goals: Know how the [[electron]], [[proton]] and [[neutron]] were discovered and their properties
Understand Thomson's and Rutherford's models, and [[atomic-number]], [[mass-number]], [[isotope]]s and [[isobar]]s
Apply electromagnetic radiation, the [[photoelectric]] effect and Planck's [[quantum]] theory
Explain the hydrogen [[line-spectrum]] with Bohr's model and know its limits
Use the [[de-broglie]] equation and the [[uncertainty]] principle to explain [[orbital]]s and [[quantum-number]]s
Write electronic configurations using the [[aufbau]], [[pauli]] and [[hund]] rules

electron.def: A negatively charged particle (−1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) of mass 9.1094 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

proton.def: A positively charged (+1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) particle in the nucleus; mass 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

neutron.def: An uncharged particle in the nucleus; mass 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

nucleus.def: The tiny, dense, positive centre of an atom (protons + neutrons); radius about 10⁻¹⁵ m.

cathode-ray.def: The stream of negative particles (electrons) leaving the cathode when electricity is discharged through a gas at low pressure.

atomic-number.def: The number of protons in the nucleus.

mass-number.def: The total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons).

isotope.def: Atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

isobar.def: Atoms with the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

wavelength.def: The distance between two successive crests of a wave.

frequency.def: Number of waves passing a point per second (Hz = s⁻¹); c = νλ.

photon.def: One quantum of electromagnetic radiation; energy E = hν.

quantum.def: The smallest fixed amount of energy that can be absorbed or emitted.

photoelectric.def: Ejection of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it.

work-function.def: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a metal; W₀ = hν₀.

threshold.def: Light below this frequency ejects no electrons, however intense.

spectrum.def: The pattern obtained when radiation is separated by wavelength.

line-spectrum.def: A spectrum of a few bright lines at fixed wavelengths; unique to each element.

ground-state.def: The lowest-energy state of an atom.

excited-state.def: Any state of higher energy than the ground state.

de-broglie.def: The wavelength associated with a moving particle: λ = h / mv.

uncertainty.def: Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly at once: Δx · Δp ≥ h / 4π.

wavefunction.def: A solution of the Schrödinger equation; |ψ|² gives the probability density of finding the electron at a point.

orbital.def: The wave function of an electron in an atom; the region around the nucleus where it is likely to be found.

quantum-number.def: The numbers n, l, mₗ (and mₛ for spin) that describe an orbital's size, shape and orientation.

shell.def: All orbitals with the same n (K, L, M, N …); n² orbitals.

subshell.def: Orbitals of the same l within a shell (s, p, d, f); (2l + 1) orbitals.

node.def: A region where the probability of finding the electron is zero; radial nodes = n − l − 1, angular nodes = l.

degenerate.def: Orbitals of equal energy (e.g. the three 2p orbitals).

shielding.def: Reduction of the nucleus's pull on outer electrons by the inner electrons.

zeff.def: The nuclear charge actually felt by an electron after shielding.

aufbau.def: Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first, then higher ones in order.

pauli.def: No two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers equal; at most 2 electrons per orbital, with opposite spins.

hund.def: In degenerate orbitals electrons first occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, and pair up only afterwards.

valence.def: Electrons in the outermost shell (highest n); the rest are core electrons.

exchange.def: Energy released when electrons of the same spin swap positions; greatest in half-filled and filled sets.

blocks.text: Dalton thought atoms indivisible, but electrification of glass or ebonite by rubbing and the passage of electricity through gases showed that atoms are built from smaller particles: the [[electron]], [[proton]] and [[neutron]].

**Discovery of the electron.** Faraday's electrolysis experiments hinted that electricity is particulate. In the late 1800s scientists applying high voltage across a low-pressure gas in a glass tube (the cathode-ray discharge tube) found [[cathode-ray]]s leaving the cathode. They travel in straight lines from cathode to anode, are invisible themselves (they make a fluorescent screen glow), bend in electric and magnetic fields like negative particles, and behave identically whatever the cathode material or gas. So they are a universal constituent of matter — the electron.

**Charge-to-mass ratio.** In 1897 J. J. Thomson measured the deflection of cathode rays in electric and magnetic fields and obtained e / mₑ = 1.758820 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹. Millikan's oil-drop experiment gave the electron charge e = −1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and showed charge always comes in whole multiples of e (q = n e). Hence mₑ = e ÷ (e/mₑ) = 9.1094 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

**Proton and neutron.** In 1886 Goldstein, using a perforated cathode, found a stream of positive particles (canal rays); the lightest, from hydrogen, is the proton (about 1836 times the electron's mass). In 1932 James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with α-particles and found an uncharged particle as heavy as the proton: the neutron.
The e/m of cathode-ray particles does not depend on the cathode material or the gas in the tube, so every atom contains the same electrons.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.text: Atoms contain electrons, protons and neutrons. How are they arranged? A model must explain why atoms are stable, why elements differ in properties, and how atoms absorb and emit radiation.

**Thomson's model (1898).** The atom is a positively charged sphere (diameter about 10⁻¹⁰ m) with electrons embedded in it like raisins in a plum pudding or seeds in a watermelon. The positive charge is spread evenly and the total charge is zero. It explained neutrality but failed later experiments.

**Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment (1909–1911).** Under Rutherford's direction, Geiger and Marsden fired a beam of positively charged α-particles (He²⁺, mass ≈ 4 u) at a very thin (about 100 nm) gold foil; a zinc-sulphide screen flashed where particles landed.

items: A small number were deflected through small angles.
A very small number rebounded at about 180°.

blocks.name: rutherford
blocks.title: α-particles and the nucleus
blocks.caption: Watch how particles bend near the nucleus; use 'Fire close-up particles' to see near head-on collisions.

blocks.text: **Conclusions — Rutherford's nuclear model:** (i) most of the atom is empty space, so most α-particles pass through; (ii) all the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny centre — the [[nucleus]] (radius ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m against ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m for the atom); (iii) electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular **orbits**, like planets round the sun; (iv) electrons and nucleus are held by electrostatic attraction.

**Drawbacks of Rutherford's model.** (1) By Maxwell's theory an electron moving in a circle (accelerating) must radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus (in about 10⁻⁸ s) — yet atoms are stable. (2) The model says nothing about how electrons are arranged or what energies they have.

sections.title: Atomic number, mass number, isotopes and isobars

blocks.text: The number of protons in the nucleus is the [[atomic-number]] (Z); a neutral atom also has Z electrons. Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons, and their total is the [[mass-number]] (A).

blocks.label: Relations
blocks.text:
Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom
A = Z + n (n = number of neutrons)
Symbol:  ᴬ_Z X  (example: ¹⁴₇N)

**[[isotope]]s**: same Z, different A. Hydrogen has three: protium (¹H, A = 1; 99.985% in nature), deuterium (²H or D, A = 2) and tritium (³H or T, A = 3). Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so nearly identical chemistry. Carbon has ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C — 6 protons and 6, 7, 8 neutrons.
**[[isobar]]s**: same A, different Z, e.g. ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N. They are different elements, so their chemistry differs.

blocks.name: atom-builder
blocks.title: Build an atom
blocks.caption: Change the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons to see Z, A, the charge and isotopes.

blocks.text: Example: in ⁸⁰₃₅Br protons = electrons = 35 and neutrons = 80 − 35 = 45. A particle with 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons has Z = 16 (sulphur), A = 32 and two extra electrons: ³²₁₆S²⁻.

sections.title: Electromagnetic radiation and the quantum theory

blocks.text: Before Bohr's model we need the nature of light. Maxwell showed that oscillating charges produce waves with mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic fields — electromagnetic radiation, described by [[wavelength]] (λ) and [[frequency]] (ν). In vacuum all of it travels at the same speed, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

blocks.label: Relations
blocks.text:
c = ν λ
wave number ν̄ = 1 / λ (unit m⁻¹)

blocks.name: em-spectrum
blocks.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
blocks.caption: Change the wavelength to see frequency, wave number and photon energy; the colour appears in the visible region.

blocks.text: **Black-body radiation.** A heated body emits radiation of higher frequency as it gets hotter (red → orange → white → blue). The wave theory could not explain the intensity distribution. In 1900 Max Planck proposed the [[quantum]] theory: atomic oscillators absorb or emit energy not continuously but in packets (quanta).

blocks.label: Planck's equation
blocks.text:
E = h ν = h c / λ
h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s

**Photoelectric effect.** In 1887 Hertz found that light falling on metals such as potassium, rubidium and caesium ejects electrons. Observations: (i) electrons appear instantly (no time lag); (ii) the number of electrons is proportional to the intensity; (iii) each metal has a [[threshold]] (ν₀) — below it no electrons come out, however bright; (iv) above ν₀ the electrons' kinetic energy grows with frequency but does not depend on intensity. The wave theory could not explain these.

In 1905 Einstein explained it using Planck's idea: light is a stream of [[photon]]s, each of energy hν. One photon gives its energy to one electron. Part of it (the [[work-function]] W₀ = hν₀) frees the electron; the rest becomes kinetic energy.

blocks.label: Einstein's equation
blocks.text:
h ν = h ν₀ + ½ mₑ v²
KE = h (ν − ν₀)

blocks.name: photoelectric
blocks.title: The photoelectric effect
blocks.caption: Choose a metal and vary frequency and intensity. Below ν₀ no electrons appear however intense the light.

blocks.text: Black-body radiation and the photoelectric effect show light behaving as particles; diffraction and interference show waves. So light has a **dual behaviour**: particle in some experiments, wave in others.

Energy of a mole of photons: for ν = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz, E = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴ = 3.313 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; × 6.022 × 10²³ for a mole = 1.995 × 10⁵ J ≈ 199.5 kJ. A 100 W bulb emitting 400 nm light gives ≈ 100 ÷ (4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 2.0 × 10²⁰ photons per second.
blocks.label: Worked example

blocks.text: Radiation absorbed or emitted by matter can be viewed as a [[spectrum]]. An **emission spectrum** comes from excited atoms; in an **absorption spectrum** white light shows dark lines where the substance absorbed certain wavelengths. Sunlight or a rainbow gives a continuous spectrum, but atoms give a few bright lines at fixed wavelengths — a [[line-spectrum]], unique to each element like a fingerprint. Bunsen used this to discover elements such as rubidium and caesium.
**The hydrogen line spectrum.** In 1885 Balmer found a formula for four visible lines (656, 486, 434, 410 nm); Rydberg generalised it:
**Bohr's model (1913).** Niels Bohr applied Planck's quantum idea to Rutherford's model for hydrogen and hydrogen-like (one-electron: He⁺, Li²⁺) ions, with these postulates:

items: An electron moves in circular orbits of fixed radius and energy around the nucleus. These are **stationary orbits**; it does not radiate while in one.
Energy is absorbed or emitted only when the electron jumps between orbits: ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν (Bohr's frequency rule).
The electron's angular momentum is quantised: mₑ v r = n h / 2π, n = 1, 2, 3, …

blocks.label: Results for hydrogen-like atoms
blocks.text:
Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J × Z² / n²   (for H: −13.6 eV / n²)
rₙ = 52.9 pm × n² / Z   (a₀ = 52.9 pm)
|ΔE| = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J × |1/n₁² − 1/n₂²|   (n₁, n₂ = the two orbits)

n = 1 is the [[ground-state]] (E₁ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J); higher levels are the [[excited-state]]. The negative sign means a bound electron has less energy than a free one (n = ∞, energy 0); the closer to the nucleus, the more negative. A drop to a lower level emits a photon, so transitions ending at n = 2 give the Balmer series — Bohr's theory yields the Rydberg equation.

blocks.name: bohr
blocks.title: Electron jumps and photons
blocks.caption: Pick 3 → 2: λ ≈ 656 nm, the red Balmer line. 2 → 1 gives ultraviolet (invisible).

blocks.text: **Limitations of Bohr's theory.** (i) It cannot explain spectra of multi-electron atoms (not even helium); (ii) it cannot explain the fine structure of lines or their splitting in magnetic and electric fields (Zeeman and Stark effects); (iii) it does not explain how atoms form molecules (chemical bonds); (iv) it ignores the wave nature of electrons and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle — a definite radius and speed cannot be known together.

Example: n = 5 to n = 2: ΔE = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1/4 − 1/25) = 4.58 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; ν = ΔE / h = 6.91 × 10¹⁴ Hz; λ = c / ν = 434 nm (the blue Balmer line). For He⁺ at n = 1, E = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 4 = −8.72 × 10⁻¹⁸ J and r = 52.9 ÷ 2 = 26.45 pm.
blocks.label: Worked example

sections.title: Towards quantum mechanics: dual nature of matter and uncertainty

blocks.text: Bohr's limitations called for a new theory, quantum mechanics, built on two ideas: the dual nature of matter and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
**Dual behaviour of matter.** In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that matter, like light, shows wave properties. A particle of mass m moving at speed v has the [[de-broglie]]:

blocks.label: de Broglie equation
blocks.text: λ = h / m v = h / p

Experiments confirm the wave nature of electrons (diffraction by metal surfaces) and it is used in the electron microscope. But for a large object — a 0.1 kg ball at 10 m s⁻¹ — λ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ m, far too small to notice. So the wave nature matters only for tiny particles such as electrons and atoms.

blocks.name: de-broglie
blocks.title: de Broglie wavelength
blocks.caption: Pick an object and compare its λ = h/mv with atomic and nuclear sizes.

blocks.text: **Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927).** The position (x) and momentum (p = mv) of a small particle cannot both be determined exactly at the same time:

blocks.label: Statement
blocks.text: Δx · Δp ≥ h / 4π     or     Δx · Δv ≥ h / 4π m

The more exactly an electron's position is known, the more uncertain its speed. Example: if Δx = 0.1 Å (10⁻¹¹ m), Δv ≥ 5.8 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ for an electron. For a 1 mg object, Δv · Δx ≈ 5 × 10⁻²⁹ m² s⁻¹ — negligible. So an electron cannot follow a definite orbit; Bohr's fixed orbits contradict this. We speak instead of the probability of finding the electron in a region.

blocks.name: uncertainty
blocks.title: The uncertainty principle
blocks.caption: Choose a particle and vary Δx to see the minimum Δv and whether it matters.

sections.title: Quantum mechanical model of the atom

blocks.text: In 1926 Erwin Schrödinger gave an equation that includes both the wave and particle character of the electron:

blocks.label: Schrödinger equation
blocks.text: Ĥ ψ = E ψ

Here Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator, E the total energy and ψ the [[wavefunction]]. Solving it gives allowed values of E and ψ. ψ itself has no physical meaning, but ψ² (|ψ|²) gives the probability density of finding the electron at a point around the nucleus. For the hydrogen atom, three [[quantum-number]]s (n, l, mₗ) arise naturally from the solution.

The wave function of an electron in an atom is called an **[[orbital]]** (not an orbit). Each orbital has a definite energy, size and shape, and holds at most two electrons. An orbit is Bohr's fixed circular path; an orbital is a probability distribution.

head: Quantum number
Name
Allowed values
What it decides
rows: the [[shell]] (K, L, M, N); size and main energy

blocks.text: The subshells l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are called **s, p, d, f**. A subshell has (2l + 1) orbitals; the nth shell has n² orbitals and at most 2n² electrons. Example: n = 3 has l = 0, 1, 2, i.e. 3s (1), 3p (3), 3d (5) = 9 orbitals.

blocks.name: quantum-explorer
blocks.title: From n to l and mₗ
blocks.caption: Change n to see the subshells and the number of orbitals.

blocks.text: **Shapes of orbitals.** Shape depends on l: s orbitals are spherical; the three p orbitals (pₓ, p_y, p_z) are dumbbells at right angles; the five d orbitals (d_xy, d_yz, d_zx, d_x²−y², d_z²) are mostly four-lobed. 1s and 2s are both spherical, but 2s is larger. A boundary-surface diagram encloses the region with about 90% probability of finding the electron.

blocks.name: orbitals
blocks.title: 3-D shapes of orbitals
blocks.caption: Pick an orbital and drag to rotate it. Red and blue are the opposite signs of ψ.

blocks.text: **Nodes.** A [[node]] is where the probability of finding the electron is zero. Radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes (planes) = l; total nodes = n − 1. 1s has none, 2s has 1, 3s has 2; 2p has one angular (planar) node.

blocks.name: nodes
blocks.title: Counting nodes
blocks.caption: Pick an orbital and see its radial and angular nodes.

blocks.text: **In hydrogen** an orbital's energy depends only on n: 1s < 2s = 2p < 3s = 3p = 3d < 4s = 4p = 4d = 4f; orbitals of equal energy are [[degenerate]]. **In multi-electron atoms**, electron-electron repulsion makes energy depend on both n and l: inner electrons [[shielding]] the outer ones, which therefore feel a smaller [[zeff]]. An s orbital penetrates closer to the nucleus and is shielded least, so energy rises s < p < d < f.

To fix the order, use the **(n + l) rule**: the orbital with the lower (n + l) has lower energy; if (n + l) is equal, the one with lower n is lower. Example: 4s (4 + 0 = 4) lies below 3d (3 + 2 = 5), so 4s fills first.

blocks.name: nl-rule
blocks.title: The (n + l) rule
blocks.caption: Choose two subshells and see which has the lower energy.

blocks.text: Electrons fill orbitals according to three rules:

items: **[[aufbau]]:** electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first. Order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p.
**[[pauli]]:** at most 2 electrons per orbital, with opposite spins (↑↓). So s, p, d, f subshells hold at most 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons.
**[[hund]]:** in degenerate orbitals (p, d, f) electrons first occupy separate orbitals with the same spin and pair up afterwards. So nitrogen's 2p holds three unpaired electrons.

blocks.text: Configurations are written as 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ (O, Z = 8) or with orbital boxes. Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ = [Ne] 3s¹; K = [Ar] 4s¹; Ca = [Ar] 4s²; Sc = [Ar] 3d¹ 4s². Electrons in the outermost shell are [[valence]] electrons, the inner ones core electrons (in Na, 3s¹ is valence and [Ne] is core).

blocks.name: aufbau
blocks.title: Fill the electrons one by one
blocks.caption: Change Z or press 'Next electron' to watch orbitals fill; note the number of unpaired electrons.

blocks.text: **Exceptions.** Cr (Z = 24) is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu (Z = 29) is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ — not 3d⁴ 4s² or 3d⁹ 4s². Half-filled (d⁵) and completely filled (d¹⁰) subshells are extra stable, and 3d and 4s are close in energy. The causes: (i) symmetrical distribution of electrons (less shielding) and (ii) larger [[exchange]] energy.
Electronic configuration decides an element's chemistry; the periodic table and bonding are explained on that basis in modern chemistry.
blocks.label: Remember

summary: Atoms consist of electrons, protons and neutrons. Z = protons, A = protons + neutrons; isotopes share Z, isobars share A.
Rutherford's α-scattering overturned Thomson's model; the nuclear model could not explain stability.
c = νλ; E = hν; in the photoelectric effect hν = hν₀ + ½mv² — the particle nature of light.
In Bohr's model Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (Z²/n²); it explains the hydrogen line spectrum but fails for multi-electron atoms.
λ = h/mv; Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π. Hence no fixed electron orbit — the Schrödinger equation and orbitals.
Four quantum numbers n, l, mₗ, mₛ; a shell has n² orbitals; l = 0, 1, 2, 3 ⇒ s, p, d, f; nodes = n − 1.
The Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules give electronic configurations; Cr and Cu are exceptions.
